solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: March 1917

parts.note: surface reading: a month and year, perhaps of a wartime event
setter's reading: the birth date of an American confessional poet, born in Boston on 1 March

explanation.walkthrough: The four bare dates in this puzzle are birth months and years of writers; this one is the poet of Life Studies and Lord Weary's Castle.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Lowell, the American poet, was born in Boston at the start of that spring month during the First World War.

clue.text: It's complementary to what Dava Sobel described

definitions.text: It's complementary to what Dava Sobel described

parts.note: surface reading: something that goes well alongside, or completes, another thing
setter's reading: Sobel's bestseller Longitude, so the partner coordinate measured north or south

explanation.surface: Something that pairs neatly with the subject of a popular science writer's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Dava Sobel's 1995 book Longitude told how John Harrison's clocks solved the east-west problem at sea; the other map coordinate completes the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Position on the globe is fixed by two coordinates, one east-west and one north-south, each needing the other.

clue.text: One with whom Tam's wife said he might be catched

definitions.text: One with whom Tam's wife said he might be catched

parts.words: One with whom Tam's wife said he might be catched
parts.note: surface reading: a jealous wife's warning about the company her husband keeps

parts.words: Tam's wife said he might be catched
parts.note: setter's reading: in Burns's Tam o' Shanter, Kate foretold he'd be caught with sorcerers by Alloway's haunted kirk

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns's poem has Tam's wife Kate prophesy that he would be 'catch'd wi' warlocks in the mirk'; he duly stumbles on a witches' dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A male witch or sorcerer, the kind of uncanny company Kate predicted her drunken husband would meet at night.

clue.text: "… who, vassals sworn, 'Gainst their — had weapon borne" (Sir Walter Scott)

definitions.text: "… who, vassals sworn, 'Gainst their — had weapon borne" (Sir Walter Scott)

parts.words: "… who, vassals sworn, 'Gainst their — had weapon borne"
parts.note: surface reading: lines of verse about sworn vassals taking up arms, with a gap
setter's reading: the source names the Scottish poet and novelist whose verse the gap belongs to

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: a vassal swore loyalty to a feudal superior, so bearing arms against him was treason.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal superior to whom vassals owed allegiance and service, exactly whom sworn vassals should never fight.

clue.text: Note a scowl developing about BP's regulations

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes around the other
something developing is still taking shape, so these letters form a new pattern

parts.note: taken as written
ut is the old name for the first note of the sol-fa scale, later doh

explanation.surface: A frown forming over the rules of an oil company.
explanation.walkthrough: BP looks like the oil company, but it is Robert Baden-Powell, founder of the Scout movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Baden-Powell drew up the code of conduct that every Scout promises to keep, so it is his movement's rulebook.

clue.text: Bloomer made at the end of a pilgrimage, a real beauty by the sound of it

parts.note: the cathedral city where Chaucer's pilgrims were heading

indicators.note: judging by the sound means the spelling is set aside and only the spoken word counts

parts.note: a belle is a beautiful woman

explanation.surface: A blunder committed at the end of a pilgrimage, by someone who sounds very pretty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' suggests a mistake, but it is a flowering plant. Chaucer's pilgrims travel to Becket's shrine in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is anything that flowers, and this tall campanula with bell-shaped blossoms is a garden flower.

clue.text: House lacking nothing demolished right at the end

definitions.text: House lacking nothing demolished right at the end

indicators.note: placed at the end means attached after everything else in the answer
a demolished building is knocked to pieces, so the remaining letters are rebuilt in another order
to lack something is to be without it, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A building with nothing missing is knocked down, rightly, in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes Poe's story The Fall of the House of Usher, where the mansion cracks and sinks into the tarn in the final lines.
explanation.definitionFit: In Edgar Allan Poe's tale the ancestral mansion of Roderick Usher collapses as the narrator flees at the close.

clue.text: Dilutee endlessly taking part of device to be destroyed?

definitions.text: Dilutee endlessly taking part of device to be destroyed?

indicators.note: without its end, the final letter is cut off
something destroyed is broken up, so the letters are smashed and rearranged

parts.note: the word with its final letter removed

indicators.note: only a part is wanted, here the opening letter of the word

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dilutee, an unskilled worker brought in to replace skilled hands, takes apart a machine to be wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue pictures the machine-breaker himself, smashing the device that threatens his trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Luddites were early nineteenth-century textile workers who wrecked new machinery they believed was destroying their livelihoods.

clue.text: June 1867

parts.note: surface reading: a month and year in the Victorian era
setter's reading: the birth date of a famous American architect, born in Wisconsin on 8 June

explanation.walkthrough: Like the other bare dates, this is a birth month and year; it pairs with 26 across to give Frank Lloyd Wright.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Lloyd Wright, designer of Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum, was born in early summer of that year.

clue.text: Gets the wrong idea about break in film accompanying start of "Saboteur"

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: a mist is a thin film, as on glass
to sunder is to break apart
and joins one thing to another

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone misreads a Hitchcock thriller, perhaps during the interval of Saboteur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' and 'Saboteur' point to cinema, Saboteur being a 1942 Hitchcock film, but film here is a thin layer of vapour.
explanation.definitionFit: To misunderstand is to interpret something wrongly, the same as forming a mistaken notion of it.

clue.text: Like one who represented part of Romanticism in nature?

definitions.text: Like one who represented part of Romanticism in nature?

parts.words: Like one who represented part of Romanticism
parts.note: surface reading: resembling some figure who stood for one strand of the Romantic movement

parts.words: represented part of Romanticism in nature
parts.note: setter's reading: in the manner of the English painter who depicted landscape and sea in the Romantic style

explanation.walkthrough: 'Represented' means depicted in paint rather than stood for: J. M. W. Turner painted storms, light and landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes art in the style of Turner, the leading English Romantic painter of natural scenes.

clue.text: One who went on a trip with Leon Uris?

definitions.text: One who went on a trip with Leon Uris?

parts.words: One who went on a trip with Leon Uris
parts.note: surface reading: a travelling companion of the American novelist
setter's reading: Uris wrote a novel called The Haj, named after the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' is not a holiday but the pilgrimage that gives Uris's 1984 novel its title.
explanation.definitionFit: A Muslim who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca may take this title, so one who went on that journey.

clue.text: July 1817

parts.note: surface reading: a month and year in the Regency period
setter's reading: the birth date of the author of Walden, born in Concord, Massachusetts on 12 July

explanation.walkthrough: Another birth month and year: the American essayist who lived by Walden Pond and wrote Civil Disobedience.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau, the Transcendentalist writer, was born in the middle of that summer month in Concord.

clue.text: After discovering arsphenamine, he turned wealthy, gaining Nobel at last

definitions.text: After discovering arsphenamine, he turned wealthy, gaining Nobel at last

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to gain something is to take it in, so one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: a synonym

indicators.note: the last of a word is only its closing letter

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A scientist finds a drug, grows rich and wins the Nobel prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsphenamine, sold as Salvarsan, was the first effective treatment for syphilis, found in Paul Ehrlich's laboratory in 1909; the whole clue describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Ehrlich, the German scientist, developed the arsenic compound and shared the 1908 Nobel prize for medicine.

clue.text: Look over entry for "kings" in dictionary

indicators.note: something turned over is upside down, so its letters run the other way
an entry is a way in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Someone checks the dictionary entry for the word 'kings'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look over' reads as one phrase meaning examine, but the definition is just 'Look' and 'over' reverses the dictionary. Dekko is British slang from Hindi for a quick look.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a dekko is informal British for taking a glance, borrowed by soldiers from a Hindi verb meaning see.

clue.text: Capital chap featuring in one of James's short stories?

definitions.text: Capital chap featuring in one of James's short stories?

parts.words: Capital chap featuring in one of James's short stories
parts.note: surface reading: an excellent fellow in a tale by Henry James
setter's reading: a man from the Irish capital, as in James Joyce's collection of stories

explanation.walkthrough: 'James' suggests Henry James, but it is James Joyce, whose 1914 story collection is Dubliners; 'capital' means of a capital city, not splendid.
explanation.definitionFit: An inhabitant of the Irish capital, and any of the characters in Joyce's collection is one.

clue.text: Did they achieve Cooper's goal at any price?

definitions.text: Did they achieve Cooper's goal at any price?

parts.note: surface reading: a question about who reached some writer's ambition
setter's reading: the goal is to live for ever, sought at any cost, so those who reached it are deathless

explanation.walkthrough: The question invites the solver to name those who succeeded in the quest for eternal life, whatever it cost.
explanation.definitionFit: Beings who never die, such as the gods of myth or authors whose fame lasts, have won lasting life.

clue.text: Fair gentleman taking time to knock back a shandy

definitions.note: the first name of Laurence Sterne's narrator Shandy

indicators.note: to knock something back is to send it the way it came, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: a mart is a market or fair
the title of a knight or gentleman
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A fair-haired gentleman takes his time downing a beer and lemonade.
explanation.walkthrough: A shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, which 'knock back' supports, but here it is a member of the Shandy family in Sterne's novel Tristram Shandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Sterne's comic novel is the life and opinions of its narrator, whose forename identifies him among the Shandy family.

clue.text: Schubert fantasy that makes us stick to one key at start of recapitulation, and again

parts.note: a wand is a slender stick
E is one of the musical keys

indicators.note: the start of a word is just its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word
the previous two letters repeated

explanation.surface: A piano fantasy that keeps us in one key, coming back at the recapitulation, and again.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface makes 'key' and 'recapitulation' look like analysis, but the key is a single letter and 'and again' repeats the last pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Schubert's Fantasy in C major for piano takes its nickname from his song Der Wanderer, quoted in its slow section.

clue.text: Dash madly about on behalf of precocious young flowering author

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps the other
acting madly means wildly and without order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
a synonym

explanation.surface: Someone rushes about wildly for the sake of a gifted child writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowering' hints at her first name, Daisy: Daisy Ashford wrote The Young Visiters at the age of nine, published in 1919.
explanation.definitionFit: Daisy Ashford was a child novelist, so precocious and young, and her first name is a flower.

clue.text: Starting out on run after getting test certificate — Mr Toad's should have had one

definitions.note: elliptical: Mr Toad's car, possessive standing for the vehicle

indicators.note: in an across answer, sitting on something means coming after it, so the earlier piece is placed second

parts.note: the MOT is Britain's annual roadworthiness test for cars

indicators.note: the starting part of a word is its first letter only

parts.note: the first letter of the word
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A reckless driver sets off after passing a roadworthiness test, which Toad of Toad Hall clearly never did.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Wind in the Willows Mr Toad crashes car after car; the tail jokes that his should have passed the British test.
explanation.definitionFit: Toad's obsession in Kenneth Grahame's novel is the motor car, so his vehicle is a motor.

clue.text: "… while human tongues — to speak" (Shelley)

parts.note: surface reading: a fragment of verse about people unable to speak, with a gap
setter's reading: the source names the Romantic poet whose line supplies the missing verb

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the missing verb completes Shelley's line, describing tongues too awed or afraid to speak steadily.
explanation.definitionFit: To shake or quiver with fear or emotion, as a nervous speaker's voice does when barely able to talk.

clue.text: Lover that's about to be betrayed

indicators.note: to be about something is to go round it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is
to sell someone out is to betray them

explanation.surface: A lover on the brink of being two-timed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a betrayed sweetheart, which suits Wagner's heroine, whose love for Tristan betrays King Mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolde is the Irish princess of the Tristan legend and Wagner's opera, one of literature's great doomed lovers.

clue.text: Hero of Begley's book about Jack Nicholson?

definitions.text: Hero of Begley's book about Jack Nicholson?

parts.note: surface reading: a biography of the film actor
setter's reading: the title character of Louis Begley's 1996 novel, whose title begins with 'About', played on film in 2002 by Nicholson

explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is part of the title, not 'concerning': the novel's hero Warren Schmidt was played on screen by Jack Nicholson.
explanation.definitionFit: The retired lawyer Albert Schmidt is the protagonist of Begley's novel, a role Nicholson took in the film version.

clue.text: Film company shortly featuring archaeologist Jones, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is the spoken word, so a different spelling with the same sound is wanted

parts.note: Indiana Jones, the film archaeologist, is known as Indy

explanation.surface: A film studio briefly casts the whip-cracking archaeologist hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' belongs to the definition: the answer is the clipped form of independent film company.
explanation.definitionFit: An indie is a small independent production company, the abbreviation used for studios outside the major ones.

clue.text: February 1917

parts.note: surface reading: the month of the first Russian revolution
setter's reading: the birth date of the Manchester-born author of A Clockwork Orange, born on 25 February

explanation.walkthrough: 'February 1917' suggests the Russian revolution, but like the other dates it is a writer's birth month and year.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Burgess, novelist and composer, was born in Manchester late in that winter month during the war.

clue.text: Frankly, seen with 8, by George!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the middle name between Frank and 8 down in the architect's name
second meaning: the name placed by George in the Liberal prime minister's surname

explanation.walkthrough: 'Frankly' and 'by George!' look like exclamations, but they place the name after Frank and before George: Frank Lloyd Wright and David Lloyd George.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh name appears both in the architect's full name and in the double-barrelled surname of the wartime prime minister.

clue.text: Brown laurel we missed developing here, that's plain

indicators.note: something developing is changing shape, so the letters are rearranged
what is missed is left out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A laurel bush has gone brown because it was not tended, which is obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's plain' reads as 'that's obvious', but plain is a stretch of flat land. The name is Latin for no tree, which suits a dead laurel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nullarbor Plain is a vast, flat, treeless limestone expanse in southern Australia crossed by the transcontinental railway.

clue.text: Weird dirge set by Goethe's spirit

indicators.note: something weird is strange and distorted, so the letters come out oddly ordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A strange funeral song set to music by Goethe, about a ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set by Goethe' suggests a musical setting, but 'set' is part of the fodder and 'by' merely joins it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In Faust, Part One, the Earth Spirit appears when Faust summons it, overwhelming him; German Erde means earth.

clue.text: From Villa d'Este emerges with credit

indicators.note: taken from within a phrase, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the last two words

explanation.surface: Someone comes out of the famous Renaissance villa at Tivoli with honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emerges' looks like the hidden indicator, but it supplies the last two letters; 'From' does the signalling. The Villa d'Este is near Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Credit in the sense of good reputation or high regard is a synonym for respect and admiration.
